issues.issue: The Declarations identify "the Insurer" as the single stock company listed above, but the Signatures endorsement prints two stock companies (Illinois Union and Westchester Surplus Lines) as issuers. Which entity is "the Insurer" bound by the policy is therefore not settled by this provision alone.

The Declarations state that only claims first made and reported to the Insurer during the policy period are covered, which cannot be squared with Insuring Agreements I.A. and I.B. and Definition V.J., which allow a claim to be reported during an "extended reporting period" after the policy period. A court would have to decide whether the capitalised Declarations notice or the insuring agreements controls the reporting deadline.

This notice says remediation-cost coverage exists only for pollution conditions first discovered AND reported in writing during the policy period, while Section VII.A. requires only written notice "as soon as practicable". The two cannot both fix the reporting deadline for a condition discovered near expiry.

The Declarations state flatly that legal defense expenses erode the Limits of Liability and any applicable self-insured retention, but Endorsement 6 creates a separate $2,000,000 Dedicated Aggregate Sublimit for legal defense expense and re-writes III.D. Which structure governs defense expense is not resolved by this notice.

This clause lists the documents that constitute the policy but supplies no order of precedence, and the instrument contains endorsements that purport to delete and replace the same provision inconsistently (Endorsement 8 and Endorsement 11 both replace Definition V.F.; Endorsement 5 and Endorsement 10 both replace Insuring Agreement I.A.). A court asked which text governs has nothing in this provision to work with.

The Coverage A policy-period entry is garbled and incomplete ("Policy Expiration Bate", "local time or the acdress"), so the clause does not identify whose local time or which address fixes 12:01 A.M. The inception and expiration moments are therefore indeterminate on the face of the item.

The limit is expressed "per 'pollution condition'" without any statement of how conditions are counted across the twelve scheduled locations, a question left to II.B and II.C's "same, continuous, repeated, or related" language. How many per-condition limits apply to a single spreading event is therefore open.

The Coverage A aggregate of $9,000,000 cannot be squared with Item 4.'s Total Policy Aggregate of $7,000,000, which Section II.G. makes the maximum liability for all coverages. A court would have to decide whether the Coverage A aggregate is illusory above $7,000,000.

The retention is stated "per 'pollution condition'" while Section II.B. collapses all related conditions into one retention, so the number of retentions payable for a multi-site event is not fixed by this item. The interaction decides whether one $100,000 retention or twelve apply.

The Coverage B policy-period entry is garbled and incomplete ("local fe or the arenes"), leaving the time-zone/address reference for the 12:01 A.M. inception and expiration unstated. On its face the item does not fix the moment coverage begins or ends.

The Coverage B aggregate of $5,000,000 taken with the Coverage A aggregate of $9,000,000 exceeds Item 4.'s $7,000,000 Total Policy Aggregate that Section II.G. makes the ceiling. The two aggregates and the total cannot all be given effect.

The $7,000,000 Total Policy Aggregate is smaller than the Coverage A aggregate of $9,000,000 in Item 2.c., yet Section II.G. is expressly "subject to" Subsections C. through F. which make Items 2.c. and 3.c. maxima. Which figure caps the Insurer's liability is a direct conflict.

Item 5. deems the premium 100% minimum-earned on the first day of the policy period, which cannot be squared with IX.A.3.'s provision for "remaining unearned premium" earned pro rata and refunded within thirty days of cancellation. On the Item 5. figure there can never be unearned premium for IX.A.3. to refund.

The grant is made "in reliance upon all statements made in the Application", which read with IX.F.'s conversion of those statements into warranties and Exclusion VI.G.'s narrower misrepresentation exclusion leaves the consequence of an inaccurate application statement unresolved. Whether an inaccuracy voids the policy or merely excludes a claim turns on reading the three together.

This Coverage A insuring agreement is deleted and replaced twice over — by Endorsement 5 for Retroactive-Date locations and by Endorsement 10 "in its entirety" — so three inconsistent versions of the grant appear in the instrument. Which text supplies the trigger for Coverage A is squarely contestable.

"First commence, in their entirety, during the 'policy period'" gives no rule for a pollution condition that develops progressively or whose commencement cannot be dated, and "in their entirety" has no stated measure. Whether a condition detected during the term "commenced in its entirety" within it is the natural battleground.

Coverage B insures pre-existing pollution conditions, yet Exclusion VI.K. (Known Conditions) bars claims and remediation costs for conditions in existence and reported to a "responsible person" before the policy period, with carve-backs keyed to a Schedule of Known Conditions Endorsement that is not attached. How much of Coverage B survives Exclusion K. is a question only the whole instrument answers.

"First commenced, in whole or part, prior to the 'policy period'" turns coverage on when a pollution condition "commenced", a term the Policy never defines or dates. For migrating or continuing contamination the commencement point is indeterminate.

"Under no circumstances shall the Insurer be liable to pay any amount within the 'self-insured retention'" cannot easily be squared with III.A.'s duty to defend and III.D.'s direction that legal defense expenses "shall be applied to the 'self-insured retention'". Whether the Insurer funds defense inside the retention is a direct tension.

"Same, continuous, repeated, or related 'pollution condition'" supplies no boundary for relatedness, and nothing says whether conditions at different scheduled locations can be "related". The number of retentions (and, through II.C.–F., of limits) turns on that undefined word.

This subsection is deleted in its entirety and replaced by Endorsement 6, whose version omits "legal defense expense" from the per-condition limit. Both texts remain printed in the instrument, so which per-condition cap applies to defense expense is contestable.

This subsection is deleted and replaced by Endorsement 6's Subsection D., which drops "legal defense expense" from the Coverage A aggregate. The instrument therefore carries two inconsistent statements of what the Item 2.c. aggregate caps.

This subsection is deleted and replaced by Endorsement 6's Subsection E., which adds a limitation to conditions "resulting from 'covered operations'" absent here. Which version fixes the Coverage B per-condition limit cannot be told from this text.

This subsection is deleted and replaced by Endorsement 6's Subsection F., which conditions the Coverage B aggregate on "covered operations" and omits legal defense expense. The two texts cannot both govern Item 3.c.

The Total Policy Aggregate is made "subject to" Subsections C. through F., yet the Item 4. figure of $7,000,000 is lower than the Item 2.c. aggregate of $9,000,000 those subsections make maxima. The subordination language and the numbers point in opposite directions.

The deeming rule turns on whether a later-reported condition is "continuous, repeated, or related" to one reported in this period, an undefined relatedness test, and it purports to declare that "no other policy shall respond" — including the prior-year policy this one renews. Both the relatedness boundary and the reach of that declaration are open on the words used.

This duty-to-defend subsection is deleted and replaced by Endorsement 6's Subsection A., which ends the duty on exhaustion of the Dedicated Aggregate Sublimit rather than of the Limits of Liability. Two different exhaustion triggers for the same duty appear in the instrument.

The provision gives the Insurer "the right to select legal counsel" while forbidding selection "without the consent of the 'insured'", and says nothing about what happens if consent is withheld or delayed. It also strips coverage for any defense expense incurred before the Insurer selects counsel, leaving pre-tender costs in dispute.

The rate cap turns on what the Insurer "actually pays to counsel that the Insurer normally retains ... when defending 'claims' or lawsuits of similar complexity", none of which is defined or verifiable from the Policy. "Similar complexity" and "reasonable proximity" have no applicable boundary.

This subsection is deleted in its entirety and replaced by Endorsement 4's Subsection C., which extends it to a "catastrophe management firm". Both texts remain printed, so which consent regime governs consultant retention is contestable.

This subsection is deleted and replaced by Endorsement 6's Subsection D., which makes defense expense erode a Dedicated Aggregate Sublimit and the Item 4. aggregate rather than Items 2., 3. and 4. Which erosion rule applies to defense expense cannot be resolved from this text.

The consequence of refusing a recommended settlement depends on whether the settlement "does not impose any additional unreasonable burdens on the 'insured'", a standard the Policy never defines. Whether the duty to defend ended therefore turns on an undefined qualifier.

The territory clause limits coverage to conditions located and claims made "within the United States of America", which sits awkwardly with Definition V.I.'s inclusion of "provincial" environmental law and Endorsement 15's provision for service of suit by a Canadian-resident insured. Read as a whole the instrument contemplates exposures the territory clause excludes.

An "additional insured" is said to hold "only those rights that are specified by endorsement", but Endorsement 2 grants rights solely for vicarious liability while Definition V.O. makes any additional insured an "insured" for all purposes. The extent of Hoffman Rettig's rights turns on reconciling the two.

"Any prospective medical monitoring costs that are intended to confirm any such physical injury, illness or disease" does not say whether monitoring costs are covered where no injury has manifested. "Mental anguish, emotional distress, or shock" likewise has no stated boundary.

The "certified industrial hygienist" definition operates only for "fungi" or legionella remediation, an exposure Endorsement 12 removes from "pollution condition" and excludes outright. Whether the definition has any remaining function depends on reading it with Endorsement 12.

"The written assertion of a legal right received by the 'insured' from a third-party" does not say whether an agency order, quarantine or notice of violation, or a demand for costs, is such an assertion. Whether a regulatory communication is a "claim" or merely a discovered condition is the central line this wording leaves unmarked.

This definition is deleted and replaced twice — by Endorsement 8 for non-owned disposal sites and by Endorsement 11 "in its entirety" for non-owned covered locations — producing inconsistent versions of "claim". Which text governs a given claim is unresolved.

Endorsement 10 deletes Definition V.E. and replaces it with "transportation", so "contingent transportation" no longer exists though the original Exclusion Q. carve-back refers to it. Whether contingent-transportation coverage survives at all can only be answered by reading the endorsement against this definition.

This definition is deleted and replaced by both Endorsement 8 (blanket "any non-owned disposal site") and Endorsement 11 (only sites on a Schedule of Non-Owned Disposal Sites Endorsement, which is not attached), and Item 8. points to Endorsements 5 and 11. Which list of "covered locations" governs is a genuine conflict.

"Emergency response" is confined to actions and costs "within seventy-two (72) hours following the discovery" of a condition posing an "imminent and substantial threat", neither of which is measurable from the text. When discovery occurred and whether the threat was imminent and substantial are left open.

The definition operates only where the indemnity is "explicitly included within a contract identified on the Schedule of Insured Contracts Endorsement attached to this Policy, if any", and no such schedule is attached. Read with Exclusion VI.B., the carve-back for environmental indemnity obligations may have no content.

"Environmental law" sweeps in any "guidance document" and voluntary or risk-based corrective action guidance alongside statutes and regulations, so what is "required by 'environmental law'" under Definition V.Y. has no fixed boundary. Whether non-binding guidance or an animal-health or public-health directive qualifies is left to argument.

This definition contemplates reporting a claim "first made against the 'insured' during or subsequent to the end of the 'policy period'", which cannot be squared with Insuring Agreements I.A. and I.B. requiring the claim to be first made during the policy period. Whether post-expiry claims can ever be covered turns on which text prevails.

The "first named insured" is made "the sole agent on behalf of all 'insureds'" for notices and other acts, which sits uneasily with IX.G.'s separation-of-insureds rule applying the Policy as if each named insured were the only insured. Whether an individual named insured can act for itself depends on reconciling the two.

"Fungi" is retained as a defined term although Endorsement 12 removes fungi from the definition of "pollution condition" and adds a Fungi and Legionella exclusion. Whether any fungi exposure remains insured cannot be answered from this definition alone.

"Government action" reaches only agencies "acting pursuant to the authority of 'environmental law'", leaving orders issued under animal-health, agricultural or public-health statutes outside the term. Whether a particular agency directive was issued under "environmental law" is the ambiguity.

"Illicit abandonment" requires "intentional placement, abandonment or disposal" by a person meeting three negative conditions, with no guidance on proving a stranger's intent or affiliation. The word "intentional" and the affiliation tests give the term no workable boundary.

The definition of "insured" is circular: it extends to officers, employees and members "of ... any 'insured'", using the term being defined to fix its own scope. The outer boundary of who is an insured therefore cannot be read off the definition.

"Legal defense expense" covers reasonable legal costs of investigation, adjustment or defense of claims, while Definition V.Y. separately includes "reasonable legal cost" incurred with consent as a "remediation cost". Which category a given legal bill falls into decides which limit and sublimit erode.

A "named insured" is given "the same rights ... as the 'first named insured'" subject only to the Subsection K. carve-out, yet II.A. conditions the Insurer's obligation on the first named insured's payment or evidence of payment of the retention. Whether a named insured can trigger coverage on its own turns on reading the two together.

This definition is deleted and replaced by Endorsement 8's much narrower version (permitting, bankruptcy, NPL-listing and remediation conditions). Both texts remain in the instrument, so which sites qualify as non-owned disposal sites is contestable.

"Policy period" is defined as the time identified in Item 2.a. "and/or" Item 3.a., so where the two Items differ or one coverage is cancelled it is unclear which single period the term denotes throughout the Policy. The "and/or" leaves the operative period indeterminate.

Whether a biological agent — a virus, bacterium or animal-waste borne pathogen — is a "solid, liquid, gaseous or thermal irritant, contaminant, or pollutant" is not answered by this list, which is illustrated only by smoke, soot, vapors, fumes, acids, alkalis, chemicals and wastes. The reach of "irritant, contaminant, or pollutant" beyond the enumerated industrial examples is the core ambiguity.

This definition is deleted and replaced in its entirety by Endorsement 12, which removes fungi and legionella and excludes odor. Two inconsistent definitions of the Policy's central term are printed in the same instrument.

"Property damage" includes "diminished value of tangible property owned by a third-party" and loss of use of property that is not injured, with no requirement of physical impact. Whether pure economic diminution of neighbouring property qualifies is left open by the wording.

"Remediation costs" are limited to expenses incurred "to the extent required by 'environmental law'", a qualifier that gives no guidance where cleanup or disposal is compelled by some other regulatory regime or done voluntarily. Whether a given cost was "required by 'environmental law'" is the ambiguity that decides coverage.

"Responsible person" reaches "any employee ... responsible for environmental affairs, control, or compliance at a 'covered location'", with no test for what responsibility suffices. Because Exclusions VI.G., J., K. and P. impute knowledge to such persons, the vagueness of the term decides those exclusions.

"Self-insured retention" is fixed by Items 2.d. and 3.d. "or as otherwise designated by endorsement", while Endorsement 4 states a separate Catastrophe Management-Specific Self-Insured Retention of $100,000. Whether one retention or two must be exhausted for a single event is unresolved between them.

The exclusion bars all asbestos-related claims but carves back only "remediation costs" for asbestos "discovered in soil or groundwater", leaving building-material and airborne asbestos remediation entirely excluded. The narrow carve-back against the broad exclusion invites an expressio unius argument.

The exclusion turns on liability "of others assumed by any 'insured' through contract" with an exception where liability "would have attached ... in the absence of such contract", a distinction the Policy never explains. Whether a grower or supply contract transfers assumed liability or merely restates existing liability is left to argument.

The exclusion applies where a condition first commenced after the location "had been sold, abandoned, or given away", none of which terms is defined, and "abandoned" in particular has no boundary for a location temporarily taken out of use. Whether the exclusion has been triggered turns on that undefined word.

Paragraph 1. excludes bodily injury to "[a]ny 'insured' or any employee of its parent corporation, subsidiary or affiliate" — omitting the insured's own employees, who are themselves "insureds" only while acting within the scope of their duties — and the "applies" list is mis-numbered "4." for "1.". The grammatical gap changes which employees' injuries are excluded.

"[O]r any associated 'claims' seeking exclusively injunctive relief in addition to such fines, penalties or damages" is internally incoherent — relief cannot be both exclusively injunctive and in addition to damages — and the carve-back for insurable punitive damages largely undoes the exclusion. What is excluded cannot be read off the sentence.

The exclusion covers property "in the care, custody, or control of any 'insured'", which read with Endorsement 11's "non-owned covered locations" (third-party farms producing product for the insured) leaves it unclear whether those premises are first-party property. Whose property is excluded depends on the endorsement, not on this text.

The materiality qualifier — "which would have affected the Insurer's decision" — is attached only to subparagraph 1.b., so it is unclear whether application misstatements under 1.a. or responsible-person misstatements under 2. must also be outcome-determinative. The placement of the clause changes the standard.

The carve-back depends on approval "of the Insurer at its sole discretion", which cannot be squared with IX.M.'s rule that any required consent "shall not be unreasonably withheld, delayed, conditioned, or denied". Whether the Insurer's refusal of internal-expense approval is reviewable turns on that conflict.

The unqualified exclusion of "claims made by any 'insured' against any other 'insured'" bars, on its terms, claims by employees, officers, additional insureds and the many named insureds against one another, since Definition V.O. makes them all insureds. How far the exclusion reaches is not stated.

The exclusion reaches "intentional disregard of, or knowing, willful, or deliberate non-compliance with, any law, statute, regulation, ... notice letter, instruction of any governmental agency", with no limit on the connection between the non-compliance and the loss. "Intentional disregard" and "instruction" are both without boundary.

The exclusion applies to conditions "in existence and reported to a 'responsible person'" before the policy period, without saying what form or level of detail a "report" requires, and the carve-back list is mis-numbered "4." for "1.". Whether a general awareness of contamination counts as a report is left open.

The exclusion of pre-policy known conditions cannot readily be squared with Coverage B (I.B.), which insures conditions that commenced before the policy period, particularly where no Schedule of Known Conditions Endorsement is attached. Whether Coverage B retains content after Exclusion K. is a whole-instrument question.

The lead-paint exclusion carves back only "remediation costs" for paint "discovered in soil or groundwater", leaving all other lead-paint remediation excluded. The narrow exception against the broad exclusion is the tension.

The exclusion depends on a change in use or operations that "materially increases the likelihood or severity" of a pollution condition measured against uses "identified" in the Application and underwriting materials, none of which is reproduced in the Policy. Both the baseline and the measure of material increase are undefined.

The exclusion is written for "naturally occurring materials" while its carve-back speaks of "naturally occurring substances" present "as a result of human activities or human processes", so the exclusion and the exception do not use the same term. Neither "naturally occurring" nor the human-activity carve-back has a stated boundary for biological or agricultural matter.

This exclusion is deleted in its entirety and replaced by Endorsement 8's "Disposal Sites" exclusion, which operates on a different structure and adds a Retroactive Date. Both versions remain printed, so which exclusion applies to a disposal site is contestable.

The exclusion's structure — a lead-in ending "and" followed by alternatives "1. ... ; or 2. ..." — leaves it unclear whether prior knowledge plus one of the two conditions, or all elements, are required. The mixed "and/or" conjunctions change what is excluded.

This exclusion is deleted and replaced by Endorsement 10's Vehicles exclusion, whose carve-back is for "transportation", while the carve-back here refers to "contingent transportation", a definition Endorsement 10 deleted. Which exclusion and which carve-back apply cannot be determined from this text.

The exclusion applies to conditions "attributable, whether directly or indirectly" to acts involving war or terrorism "regardless of any other cause", with "terrorism" defined to include any commission or threat of a "dangerous act" intended to further social or economic objectives. The causal reach of "indirectly" and the breadth of the defined term are both open.

Notice "as soon as practicable" cannot be squared with the Declarations and Insuring Agreements I.A./I.B., which require the discovery or claim to be reported in writing during the policy period as a condition of coverage. Whether late-but-practicable notice forfeits coverage depends on which requirement controls.

The list of cooperation duties is mis-numbered — two obligations are left unnumbered between items 2. and 5. — and item 5. requires "such information and cooperation as it may reasonably require" without limit. What the insured must do to avoid breach is not fixed by the text.

This subsection is deleted in its entirety and replaced by Endorsement 4's Section V., which adds "catastrophe management firm" and "catastrophe management costs" and drops the word "express" from the consent requirement. Two versions of the consent condition are printed in the instrument.

The Insurer may mitigate if "in the sole judgment of the insurer" the insured fails to take reasonable steps, which cannot be squared with IX.M.'s requirement that consents not be unreasonably withheld or conditioned and with III.C.'s allocation of the remediation duty to the insured. Whether the Insurer's judgment is reviewable turns on that conflict.

Entitlement to the extended reporting periods is tied to cancellation "as described in Subsection A., Paragraph 1. of Section IX." — cancellation by the first named insured — or nonrenewal, saying nothing about cancellation by the Insurer under IX.A.2. (as replaced by Endorsement 9). Whether an insurer-cancelled policy carries an extended reporting period is unresolved.

Deeming a claim reported in an extended reporting period to have been "made and reported on the last day of the 'policy period'" sits against the Declarations' statement that only claims made and reported during the policy period are covered, and against II.H.'s deeming rules. How the two deeming provisions interact for a claim made after expiry is open.

The sixty-day basic extended reporting period is deleted and replaced by Endorsement 7's ninety days, yet both texts remain printed in the instrument. Which period the insured has is a direct conflict.

This thirty-four month supplemental extended reporting period is deleted and replaced by Endorsement 7's thirty-three months, so two different maximum periods and premium mechanics appear in the Policy. Which controls the insured's purchase right is contestable.

The insured may cancel by mailing notice "stating when such cancellation shall be effective", with no minimum notice period and no rule for a notice that names no date or a retroactive date. The effective date of a cancellation is left to the notice alone.
The sixty-day cancellation notice requirement is deleted and replaced by Endorsement 9's ninety days, yet both texts are printed. How much notice the Insurer must give is a direct conflict.

The provision for "remaining unearned premium" earned pro rata and refunded within thirty days cannot be squared with Item 5.'s statement that the premium is 100% minimum-earned as of the first day of the policy period. On Item 5. there is no unearned premium for this paragraph to return.

The inspection right extends to "the 'covered locations'" and only "[t]o the extent of the 'insured's' ability to provide such access", which as amended by Endorsement 11 includes third-party non-owned covered locations the insured does not control. What access the insured owes for those sites is not settled by this text.

The audit right runs for three years after "the final termination of this Policy", a term the Policy never defines and which does not match "policy period" or the extended reporting periods. When the audit window closes is therefore indeterminate.

The bar on suing the Insurer "unless all of the Policy terms have been fully complied with" makes every term, however immaterial, a condition precedent to suit. The scope of "all of the Policy terms" is unbounded on the face of the clause.

The clause presupposes "other insurance to which this Policy is excess" and "any underlying insurer", although no underlying insurance is scheduled anywhere and IX.H. instead makes this Policy excess of all other collectible insurance. Whether this Policy is an excess layer at all can only be answered by reading the two together.

The recovery waterfall gives the insureds recovery first "to the extent of any payments in excess of the limit of coverage", using "limit of coverage" — a phrase found nowhere else, the Policy speaking of "Limits of Liability" — and then repeats "insured" for the retention. The order and measure of sharing are not clear from the words used.

Making all Declarations, schedule, endorsement and Application statements "warranties" upon which the Policy was issued cannot easily be squared with Exclusion VI.G., which treats application misrepresentation as a claim-specific exclusion, and with IX.A.2.b., which makes it a ground for prospective cancellation only. Whether an inaccuracy avoids the Policy or merely excludes a claim turns on the three read together.

The separation-of-insureds rule excepts "Cancellation condition 2.a., above", but 2.a. is non-payment of premium while the conduct-based provision that could sensibly be imputed among insureds is 2.b. (fraud or misrepresentation). The mis-citation changes whose conduct defeats separate treatment.

The clause makes this Policy excess of "other valid and collectible insurance" covering "a loss also covered by this Policy", which cannot easily be squared with the Insuring Agreements' promise to pay in excess only of the self-insured retention and with IX.D.'s reference to insurance this Policy is excess to. Whether the Policy is primary above the retention is a whole-instrument question.

The clause submits the parties to "the exclusive jurisdiction of the State of New York" while Endorsement 15 promises that, at the insured's request, the company "will submit to the jurisdiction of any court of competent jurisdiction". The two cannot both fix the forum.

The clause names a State rather than a court, requires the parties to "comply with all requirements necessary to give such court jurisdiction" without identifying any court, and then preserves removal to federal court. Whether it is a binding exclusive forum-selection clause at all is unclear from its own words.

The exception — "except as provided by endorsement and attached to this Policy" — is grammatically incomplete, leaving unclear whether a change requires an endorsement issued and physically attached, and by whom signed. The mechanism for a binding change or assignment is not stated coherently.

Headings are said to form no part of the terms, yet IX.G. identifies the operative carve-outs solely by heading ("the Fraud or Misrepresentation Exclusion", "the Known Conditions Exclusion", and others) and several endorsements identify amended provisions by heading. If headings have no effect, those cross-references lose their referents.

The general rule that any required consent "shall not be unreasonably withheld, delayed, conditioned, or denied" cannot be squared with Exclusion VI.H.'s approval "at its sole discretion" and VII.D.'s "sole judgment of the insurer". Whether those discretions are constrained is a direct conflict.

The Schedule of Named Insureds lists only "Farm Nutrients LLC", while the endorsement header and Item 1. name Rembrandt Enterprises, Inc. as the insured. Whether Rembrandt is itself a "named insured" — a status that matters under II.A., V.S. and IX.G. — is not resolved by the schedule.

The additional insured is covered "solely with respect to their vicarious liability arising out of any 'named insured's' direct liability", a formula that does not say what happens where the additional insured is alleged to be directly at fault alongside a named insured. "Vicarious liability" is undefined and does the whole work of the grant.

The grant covers business interruption loss "during a 'period of interruption' in excess of the Deductible Period", comparing a loss amount with a period of time; whether the Deductible Period bars the first three days' loss or defers coverage entirely is not stated here. The mismatch of measures makes the trigger unclear.

The condition requires the loss to be reported "during the 'policy period'" although Condition IV.B. lets the period of interruption run until operations could reasonably be restored, potentially after expiry. A loss not yet incurred by expiry cannot be reported within the period the condition demands.

The $5,000,000 sublimit is made "subject to the Limits of Liability identified in the Declarations", but those limits (Items 2., 3. and 4.) are expressed in Section II. as caps on "claims", "remediation costs" and "legal defense expense" — not on business interruption loss. How the sublimit erodes or is capped by the Declarations limits is unresolved.

The clause excludes loss "incurred during the Deductible Period" without saying when that three-day period begins — at the pollution condition, at discovery, or at suspension of operations. The start date is left indeterminate.

"Business income" mixes net profit "that would have been realized had there been no 'business interruption'" with continuing operating and payroll expense, excluding certain payroll, and with temporary rent. Whether continuing expenses are recoverable in addition to, or only within, the hypothetical profit figure is not stated.

"Business interruption" requires a "necessary partial or complete suspension" of operations, with no measure of what makes a suspension necessary or how partial a slowdown must be to count. Both qualifiers are without boundary.

"Covered pollution condition" exists only where remediation costs from first-party discovery are covered under Coverage A. or B., so Endorsement 12's Fungi and Legionella exclusion and Exclusion VI.N. (Naturally Occurring Materials) may remove the predicate entirely. Whether any business interruption coverage survives those exclusions is a whole-instrument question.

"Delay expense" applies only "for a 'covered location' under development" — a phrase never defined — and its enumerated list of additional costs (with one item left unnumbered) admits no comparable expenses. The scope of the enumerated list against unlisted delay costs is open.

"Extra expense" must be "necessary to avoid or mitigate" interruption and incurred "to actually minimize" foregone business income, with no measure for either requirement. Whether spending that failed to reduce lost income qualifies is unresolved.

"Period of interruption" fixes only when the period commences and never states when it ends, so the definition standing alone gives the loss period no outer limit. The measure of "necessarily suspended" is also unstated.

"Rental income" is keyed to a "suspension" of a rented covered location, while the coverage grant and "business income" are keyed to a "period of interruption" and "business interruption" — different defined triggers. Which trigger measures lost rent is unresolved between the definitions.

"Suspension" turns on the premises being "rendered untenantable for the purposes identified to the Insurer at the inception of the Policy", purposes that appear nowhere in the Policy documents. Both "untenantable" and the unrecorded purposes are indeterminate.

The period of interruption begins "on the date the operations would have begun" but for the condition, a wholly hypothetical date with no method of proof or benchmark. When a delayed start-up period begins is therefore open.

The second sentence withholds coverage for lost business income "as a result of unfavorable business conditions caused by the impact of the 'covered pollution condition'", which is difficult to distinguish from the market-driven loss the coverage otherwise insures. The line between covered interruption loss and excluded "unfavorable business conditions" is not drawn.

The appraisal clause is internally garbled — "A decision agreed to by the appraisers, of the umpire, if necessary, shall be binding" — and then requires each party to "[b]ear the other expenses of the appraisal and umpire equally". Whether an umpire's decision alone binds, and who pays what, cannot be read off the text.

The Insurer's retention of "all of its rights pursuant to the Policy to deny all or a portion of the claim" cannot readily be squared with Condition IV.C.'s statement that the appraisers' or umpire's decision "shall be binding upon both parties". What an appraisal actually decides is left in doubt.

The added exclusion bars business interruption loss related to "any of the individually excluded exposures identified above", but nothing "above" in this endorsement identifies excluded exposures. The phrase has no antecedent, leaving the exclusion's content to be supplied by argument.

The grant is for costs "in excess of the 'self-insured retention'", a term Definition V.AA. ties to Items 2.d. and 3.d., while this endorsement separately states a Catastrophe Management-Specific Self-Insured Retention of $100,000. Which retention must be exhausted, and whether both apply to one event, is unresolved.

The trigger is keyed to events commencing "on or after the inception date identified in Item 2.a." rather than during the "policy period" used everywhere else, and Item 2.a. governs Coverage A only. For a Coverage B condition the timing benchmark this clause supplies does not match the coverage it sits on.

The Aggregate Sublimit is made "subject to the Limits of Liability identified in the Declarations", yet those limits are expressed in Section II. as caps on claims, remediation costs and legal defense expense, not on "catastrophe management costs". Whether such costs erode Items 2.–4. is not answered here.

This replacement gives the insured "the right and the duty" to retain a consultant or catastrophe management firm, while the same endorsement's replacement of VII.C. forbids any insured from retaining one without the Insurer's prior written consent. The duty and the prohibition cannot both be performed if consent is refused.

"Adverse media coverage" requires "national or regional news exposure" that is "reasonably likely to have a negative impact" on income, reputation, community relations, public confidence or good will, none of which is measurable. Both the geographic threshold and the likelihood of harm are undefined.

The trigger depends on "the good faith opinion of a 'key executive'" that claims will exceed the retention and that services are needed, making the insured's own subjective view the coverage condition. Whether the Insurer can contest that opinion is not stated.

Item 2. is garbled ("printing, advertising, mailing of materials of public relations materials") and item 5. ends in an open catch-all — "or other necessary response costs" — after a list of medical, funeral, counseling, travel and temporary living costs. The reach of the catch-all against the enumerated specifics is the tension.

This replacement forbids any insured from retaining a consultant or catastrophe management firm without prior written consent, while the same endorsement's replacement of III.C. imposes on the insured "the right and the duty" to retain one. The two provisions of one endorsement pull in opposite directions.

The added exclusion bars catastrophe management costs related to "any of the individually excluded exposures identified above", but nothing above in this endorsement identifies any excluded exposure. The reference has no antecedent.

Every Retroactive Date in the schedule is the policy inception date (and two are typed "11/01/2074" and "41/01/2014"), which leaves nothing for paragraph 2. of the replacement Coverage A timing clause — coverage for conditions commencing before the policy period — to operate on. Whether the Retroactive-Date locations obtained any pre-inception coverage turns on that.

This replacement of Insuring Agreement I.A. is itself deleted "in its entirety" by Endorsement 10, which substitutes a version without any retroactive-date paragraph. Which text grants Coverage A at the Retroactive-Date locations is a direct conflict.

This timing clause extends Coverage A to conditions commencing before the policy period but on or after a Retroactive Date, whereas Endorsement 10's later replacement of I.A. limits Coverage A to conditions commencing entirely during the policy period. The two cannot both fix the timing of Coverage A.

"All other terms and conditions of this Policy remain unchanged" cannot be squared with Endorsement 10's deletion and replacement of the very insuring agreement this endorsement re-wrote. The boilerplate does not tell a reader which endorsement survives.

The replacement per-condition limit is expressed only for "claims" and "remediation costs", dropping "legal defense expense" that the deleted text included, while III.D. as replaced still makes defense expense erode limits. Whether Item 2.b. caps defense expense is left unclear by the omission.

This subsection makes the Item 2.c. aggregate ($9,000,000) the maximum liability, which exceeds the Item 4. Total Policy Aggregate ($7,000,000) that II.G. makes the ceiling. The two aggregates cannot both be maxima.

The Coverage B per-condition limit is confined to conditions "resulting from 'covered operations'", a quoted term that appears nowhere in Section V. or in any endorsement's definitions. The limitation has no defined content.

The Coverage B aggregate is likewise confined to conditions "resulting from 'covered operations'", a quoted term the Policy never defines. Whether the aggregate applies to all Coverage B conditions or only some cannot be told from the words used.

The duty to defend is said to end on exhaustion of the Dedicated Aggregate Sublimit, while Subsection F. added by the same endorsement has the Insurer retain a right to defend after that exhaustion and the following paragraph contemplates continued defense at the Insurer's expense eroding Item 4. Whether defense continues after the sublimit is exhausted is unresolved between them.

Defense expense is made to reduce both the Dedicated Aggregate Sublimit and the Item 4. aggregate and also to be "applied to the 'self-insured retention'", which cannot be squared with II.A.'s statement that "[u]nder no circumstances shall the Insurer be liable to pay any amount within the 'self-insured retention'". Whether the Insurer funds defense within the retention and double-erodes the limits is a direct conflict.

The $2,000,000 dedicated defense sublimit is made subject only to the Item 4. Total Policy Aggregate, while III.D. as replaced has defense expense also reduce that aggregate and be applied to the retention. How the sublimit interacts with the per-condition limits in Items 2.b. and 3.b. (also $2,000,000) is not stated.

The Insurer's retained "right, but not the duty" to defend after exhaustion sits against Subsection A. of the same endorsement, which ends the duty, and against the following paragraph giving the first named insured the right to select counsel subject to Insurer consent. Who controls the defense after exhaustion depends on reconciling the three.

The settlement sentence is garbled — "If the insurer recommends a settlement of any ongoing or future 'claim' for which it is not which is acceptable to a claimant" — so the condition on which the Insurer's liability is capped cannot be read. The mechanical defect changes, and may destroy, the operation of the cap.

The paragraph caps the Insurer's "liability for covered 'loss'", using a quoted term that this Policy never defines, whereas the rest of the instrument speaks of "claims", "remediation costs" and "legal defense expense". What the cap applies to is undefined.

This paragraph makes post-exhaustion defense expense reduce the Item 4. aggregate, which Subsection D. of the same endorsement already provides for all legal defense expense. Whether defense expense erodes Item 4. once or twice is left unresolved between them.

This ninety-day basic extended reporting period replaces Section VIII.C.'s sixty days, but both texts remain printed in the instrument. Which period the first named insured actually has is a direct conflict.

This thirty-three month supplemental extended reporting period replaces Section VIII.D.'s thirty-four months, and both texts remain printed. Which maximum period may be purchased, on the same 200% premium, is a direct conflict.

This replacement of Definition V.F. treats "any 'non-owned disposal site'" as a covered location, whereas Endorsement 11 deletes and replaces the same definition again, limiting it to sites identified on a Schedule of Non-Owned Disposal Sites Endorsement that is not attached. Which version of "covered location" governs is a direct conflict.

This replacement of the definition of "claim" is itself deleted and replaced "in its entirety" by Endorsement 11 for non-owned covered locations, so two inconsistent definitions of "claim" and two Retroactive Dates operate in the instrument. Which text governs a given claim cannot be told from this endorsement.

Qualification as a "non-owned disposal site" turns on facts about the site at the time of disposal — whether it was "properly permitted and licensed", free of bankruptcy, unlisted on CERCLA lists, and not under remediation — none of which is defined or knowable from the Policy. Whether a site qualified is left to be litigated on each of those conditions.

Paragraph 2. excludes conditions at non-owned disposal sites which "received waste from an 'insured'" before the policy period or Retroactive Date, while the coverage clause in the replaced Definition D. is keyed to a "named insured's" waste. The mismatch between "insured" and "named insured" changes the reach of the exclusion.

This ninety-day cancellation notice replaces Section IX.A.2.'s sixty days, yet both texts remain printed in the instrument. How much notice the Insurer must give before cancelling is a direct conflict.

This endorsement deletes and replaces Insuring Agreement I.A. "in its entirety", thereby also displacing Endorsement 5's Retroactive-Date version of the same subsection, which it does not mention. Which Coverage A grant governs the Retroactive-Date locations is a direct conflict.

This timing clause limits Coverage A to conditions commencing "in their entirety, during the 'policy period'", which cannot be squared with Endorsement 5's timing clause extending Coverage A to conditions commencing before the period but after a Retroactive Date. Both endorsements are in force and only one can fix the trigger.

This replacement of Definition V.E. substitutes "transportation" for "contingent transportation", leaving the original Exclusion VI.Q. carve-back (and any expectation of contingent-transportation coverage) without a defined referent. Whether transport by a hired carrier alone, or also by an insured, is covered depends on reading the endorsements together.

The carve-back "This exclusion shall not apply to 'transportation'" is unqualified, though transportation coverage is granted only under Coverage A. as amended, not under Coverage B. or the supplemental coverages. Whether the exclusion is switched off for all coverages or only Coverage A. is unresolved.

"All other terms and conditions of this Policy remain unchanged" cannot be squared with this endorsement's silent displacement of Endorsement 5's replacement of the same insuring agreement. The boilerplate leaves the reader without a rule of priority.

This is a third replacement of Definition V.F., and it limits non-owned disposal site coverage to sites on a "Schedule of Non-Owned Disposal Sites Endorsement" that is not attached, contradicting Endorsement 8's blanket inclusion of any non-owned disposal site. Which definition of "covered location" controls is a direct conflict.

The carve-out excludes any "claim" "from or made in relation to the owner, operator, contractor of the 'non-owned covered location'; or those of their employees", and "in relation to" does not say whether it bars only claims by those persons or any claim connected with them. Given that the growers' own losses are the likely claims, the phrase decides the coverage.

"Non-owned covered locations" are sites which "pursuant to an agreement with the 'insured', produce certain egg related products on behalf of the 'insured'", and "certain egg related products" is undefined. Whether pullet-raising or other upstream activity at a scheduled site falls inside the term is left open.

"All other terms and conditions of this Policy remain unchanged" cannot be squared with this endorsement's second deletion and replacement of Definition V.F., which Endorsement 8 had already replaced. Nothing tells the reader which replacement survives.

Whether a biological agent such as a virus or pathogen borne in animal waste is a "solid, liquid, gaseous or thermal irritant, contaminant, or pollutant" is not resolved by a list illustrated only by smoke, soot, vapors, fumes, acids, alkalis, chemicals, hazardous substances and waste materials. The endorsement's express removal of "fungi", legionella and "odor" sharpens rather than answers the question of what biological matter remains within the term.

This replacement strips fungi and legionella out of "pollution condition" while Definitions V.C. (certified industrial hygienist), V.L. (fungi) and V.Y. (remediation costs, which prescribes how fungi and legionella remediation costs are established) remain in force. Whether those provisions retain any operation cannot be answered without reading them against this text.

The added exclusion bars claims and costs related to "fungi", legionella "or odor", although the same endorsement has already removed fungi, legionella and odor from the definition of "pollution condition". Whether the exclusion does independent work — for example reaching conditions that also involve other contaminants — turns on reading the two paragraphs together.

The $500,000 natural resource damage sublimit applies to "claims" and associated legal defense expense, while Definition V.X.4. makes natural resource damages a species of "property damage" subject to the Item 2.b./3.b. per-condition limits. Which cap applies to a claim mixing natural resource damage with other property damage is unresolved.

The grant covers only "claims" and associated legal defense expense arising out of product pollution, while the endorsement's Limits of Liability section caps "claims", "remediation costs" and legal defense expense arising out of product pollution. Whether remediation costs for product pollution are covered at all cannot be told from the two read together.

Paragraph 2. contains the duplicated phrase "on or after the on or after the Retroactive Date, if any", and "first commences, in its entirety" is applied to "product pollution" whose defining event is a third party's later use of the product. When product pollution "commences" is left indeterminate by the wording.

This section makes the Aggregate Product Pollution Sublimit the maximum for "claims", "remediation costs" and legal defense expense, though the insuring clause grants no remediation-cost coverage for product pollution, and the per-condition and aggregate sublimits are both $1,000,000 so that the per-condition cap has no independent effect. Whether remediation costs are within this coverage depends on reconciling the two.

The exclusion reaches anything "arising out of any goods or products manufactured, sold or distributed by an 'insured'", a causal phrase with no stated limit, with a carve-back only for "product pollution" as defined. Whether contamination at the insured's premises "arises out of" its products is left open by the breadth of the phrase.

"Product Pollution" requires a pollution condition arising out of "the use of a product ... after the 'insured' has relinquished possession", and then says "products do not include waste products" without defining waste. Whether a contaminated feed, egg or by-product is a product or a waste product decides the coverage.

The endorsement says sanctions may "prohibit us from providing insurance", using "us" although the Policy elsewhere identifies only "the Insurer" and defines no first-person parties. It also supplies no mechanism for determining when a prohibition applies.

The company's promise to "submit to the jurisdiction of any court of competent jurisdiction" at the insured's request cannot be squared with Section IX.I., which commits the parties to the exclusive jurisdiction of the State of New York. Which provision fixes the forum is a direct conflict.

The Canadian service provision presupposes an insured resident in Canada, although Section IV. limits coverage to pollution conditions located and claims made within the United States. The provision has no evident field of operation under this Policy.

The saving clause says nothing herein varies the Policy's terms "other than as above stated", leaving unresolved whether the endorsement's jurisdiction and service undertakings do override Section IX.I.'s exclusive New York jurisdiction clause. The exception swallows the reservation.
